analysis.one_liner: Imposes fines on social media companies that host child sexual abuse material and lets private citizens sue them.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its referral to the Senate Judiciary Committee, drew no cosponsors, and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it unlawful for social media companies to knowingly or recklessly host or distribute child sexual abuse material, with fines of $100,000 to $500,000 per violation. It would require every covered platform to set up a public notice system where anyone can flag such material, force a decision within 10 days, and give the flagger a written explanation if the platform refuses to act. It would also let private citizens sue on the government's behalf and keep 25% to 50% of any fine, and it would block the platforms from using their usual federal liability shield to escape these suits.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and families, if the bill speeds removal of child sexual abuse material from major platforms. Private citizens who file successful suits could recover a share of fines. The Justice Department would gain a new enforcement tool against platforms that host illegal content.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children and families, plus private plaintiffs

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful, not just against terms of service, for a social media company to knowingly or recklessly host or distribute child sexual abuse material, with civil penalties of $100,000 to $500,000 per violation.
Requires every covered platform to designate a publicly listed agent to receive abuse reports, respond within 10 days, and explain in writing why it did not remove flagged material.

Creates a private right of action, similar to whistleblower suits, letting a person sue a platform on behalf of the United States and keep at least 25% of the penalty if the government takes over, or at least 50% if the person prosecutes the case alone.
States that Section 230 of the Communications Act, the law that generally shields platforms from liability for user-posted content, cannot be used to defeat a claim under this bill.

analysis.who_pays: Social media companies, which would face fines up to $500,000 per violation, a mandatory notice-and-response bureaucracy, and loss of their Section 230 defense against these suits. If platforms respond defensively, the cost could spill onto users as more aggressive removal of borderline content.
analysis.who_pays_short: Social media companies like Meta and X

drawbacks.text: The 10-day removal deadline and the liability standard covering 'reckless' hosting could push platforms to remove material aggressively and quickly, sweeping in lawful content to avoid fines or suits.

The bounty structure pays private plaintiffs a share of fines, which critics would warn could reward activist campaigns that flood platforms with notices, including good-faith mistakes about what counts as child sexual abuse material.

The bill excludes companies whose principal function is peer-to-peer messaging, the category that includes encrypted messaging apps, so it leaves one major channel for such material largely outside its scope.
Because no other senator cosponsored it and no committee action was ever scheduled, the bill had no visible path to becoming law and no practical effect on child safety in the 118th Congress.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The goal — pressuring platforms to remove child sexual abuse material faster — is one few would oppose, and the notice-and-explanation requirement is a genuinely useful transparency tool. The enforcement design is aggressive: whistleblower-style bounties and a stripped liability shield would give platforms strong reasons to err on the side of deletion, which is the standard cost of takedown mandates. The carve-out for peer-to-peer messaging apps leaves a real gap. On balance, this is a serious child-safety proposal aimed squarely at a concentrated industry, but it was written by a single sponsor with no cosigners and never received any committee consideration.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in March 2023, and nothing further ever happened — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Josh Hawley introduced the bill on March 15, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.
No other senator cosponsored the bill during the entire two-year Congress.
The Senate Judiciary Committee took no further action, so the bill never received a hearing or a floor vote and expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Social media companies are better off: they avoided new fines, a mandatory notice-and-takedown regime, and the loss of their Section 230 liability shield, with no counterweight of new protections for children enacted in this bill's place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Social media companies that avoided liability

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.role: U.S. Senator from Missouri; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on March 15, 2023.

against.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred to the committee; it received no further action for two years.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, so it never developed a partisan profile in any recorded vote or committee action.

industries.note: The bill would put fines of $100,000 to $500,000 on platforms that host child sexual abuse material, require a public notice system with 10-day deadlines, and strip away their Section 230 defense against these suits. The industry avoided all of this when the bill died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
